title: Sikh thought close
hook: God, the self, ethics and the world, through the Guru's eyes

segments.voice: Yesterday, thinking as a Sikh today: vichar, the hukamnama, principle before proof-text. Your line was old word, new questions. What modern choice did you hold up to an old thread? Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

Plenty of what we learn slips away by the end of the week. Some ideas don't. They lodge somewhere, like a pebble in a shoe, and you keep noticing them at odd moments: in traffic, at the sink, halfway through an argument. This stretch of the path has been about Sikh thought: what the Gurus taught about God, about the self, about how to live, and about the world we share. Today it closes. Not with a test. With a walk back through the rooms, and a question at the end: which idea came home with you?
screen: `A PEBBLE IN A SHOE.` → `GOD, SELF, LIVING, WORLD.` → `WHICH IDEA CAME HOME WITH YOU?`

segments.voice: First, God. The Granth opens with Ik Onkar, the One, and you met the names: Waheguru, the Wonderful Lord, and many others drawn from many tongues. You met God with qualities and without, vast and close, beyond everything and within everyone. Second, the self. Haumai, ego, which isn't the same as you. The mind as a friend to be trained, not an enemy to be beaten. Hukam, the order, and effort inside it. Grace and deeds. This life as the chance, and the hope of being free while still living. Third, how to live. The thieves that clutch and crave: attachment, greed, desire out of place. Against them, chardi kala, rising spirits, and bhaana, accepting the will. Ardas that asks and then accepts. The portrait of the Gurmukh, humble and truthful and serving, and of the Khalsa. Fourth, the world. Equal souls. Women as equals. Force only as the last resort, justice for the wronged, truth spoken to rulers. And then the week just gone: many tongues in one script, the Word that is sung, kesh as given, the langar row, the open door, honest citizens, old words meeting new questions. Underneath all of it sits the question Guru Nanak asks in the first pauri of the Japji. In paraphrase: how do we become truthful, and how does the wall of falsehood come down? His answer: by walking in the hukam, the order written with us. Much of this stretch can be heard as unpacking that line.
screen: `GOD: ONE, NAMED IN MANY WAYS.` · `THE SELF: EGO, MIND, FREE WHILE LIVING.` · `LIVING: THIEVES, RISING SPIRITS, THE GURMUKH.` · `THE WORLD: EQUAL SOULS, AN OPEN DOOR.` · then, large: `THE IDEA THAT STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the idea that changed you. Settle, and breathe. Let the rooms go by slowly: God, the self, how to live, the world. Don't pick the idea you think you should pick. Wait for the one that has quietly been showing up in your days, the pebble in the shoe. When it comes, give it a name in a few words. Then ask: where did it show up this week? If you pray, you can offer thanks for it. If you don't, just hold it, and let it stay. The bell holds the time.
Sikh thought close. God, the self, how to live and the world, through the Guru's eyes, gathered under one question: how does the wall of falsehood come down? Today's word.
Your line: the idea that stayed. Today, tell one person the idea you named, in one or two sentences, and why it stuck. Day one thousand four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs study Gurmat, the Guru's teaching, through the Guru Granth Sahib, katha (talks explaining the hymns) in the gurdwara, and daily prayers such as the Japji, whose first pauri asks how to become truthful.
